source_lines.26: Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $k$ be a field and $n\ge1$, $G=\mathrm{GL}_n$ with standard split maximal torus $T=D_n$ of diagonal matrices and standard Borel $B$ of upper triangular matrices ([[def-root-datum-of-a-split-reductive-group]], [[thm-parabolics-and-levi-decomposition]]). The roots are $\alpha_{ij}=\chi_i-\chi_j$ ($i\neq j$) with root groups $U_{ij}=\{I+aE_{ij}\}$, and the base is $\{\alpha_{i,i+1}:1\le i\le n-1\}$, identified with $\{1,\dots,n-1\}$. For $I\subseteq\{1,\dots,n-1\}$ let $\Delta\smallsetminus I=\{a_1,a_1+a_2,\dots,a_1+\cdots+a_{s-1}\}$ with $a_i\ge1$ and $\sum a_i=n$; then $P_I$ consists of the block upper triangular matrices with diagonal blocks of sizes $a_1,\dots,a_s$, arbitrary entries above the block diagonal and zero below, the standard Levi subgroup is $L_I=\prod_i\mathrm{GL}_{a_i}$ (block diagonal) and $R_u(P_I)$ is the block upper unitriangular subgroup, with identity diagonal blocks, zero blocks below them and arbitrary blocks above them; the multiplication $R_u(P_I)\rtimes L_I\to P_I$ is an isomorphism, $I\mapsto P_I$ is a bijection onto the smooth parabolic subgroup varieties containing $B$, and $P_\varnothing=B$, $P_{\Delta}=G$. The maximal proper parabolics $P_{\Delta\smallsetminus\{i\}}$ are the stabilizers of the partial flags with a single subspace of dimension $i$, and the Bruhat cells of the complete flag variety $G/B$ are indexed by $S_n$ with $\dim Y(w)=n(w)=\#\{(i,j):i<j,\ w(i)>w(j)\}$.
source_lines.42: 2.1 Let $I\subseteq\{1,\dots,n-1\}$ and let the complement of $I$ in the ordered set of simple roots be the partial sums listed, so that the integers $a_1,\dots,a_s\ge1$ sum to $n$. Choose a cocharacter with diagonal exponents constant within each block and strictly decreasing between consecutive blocks. Entrywise conjugation scales $x_{ij}$ by the exponent difference, so its limit subgroup is precisely the group with zero blocks below the diagonal and its limit kernel has identity diagonal blocks. By [F2] its zero simple-root pairings recover $I$. Thus $P_I$ is the group of invertible matrices preserving the flag of subspaces $0\subseteq k^{a_1}\subseteq k^{a_1+a_2}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq k^n$, i.e. the block upper triangular matrices with diagonal blocks of sizes $a_1,\dots,a_s$; its unipotent radical $R_u(P_I)$ has identity diagonal blocks, zeros below and arbitrary blocks above and its Levi factor is the block diagonal $\prod_i\mathrm{GL}_{a_i}$; the multiplication map $R_u(P_I)\rtimes L_I\to P_I$ is a group-scheme isomorphism by [F2], and $P_\varnothing=B$ and $P_{\Delta}=G$ because the corresponding flags are the complete flag and the trivial flag. The all-algebra matrix equations verify these stabilizers scheme-theoretically. For $n=1$ the simple-root set is empty, both endpoints are $G=B=\mathbf G_m$, and its unipotent radical is trivial. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]
source_lines.44: 3.1 The maximal proper parabolics correspond to $I=\Delta\smallsetminus\{i\}$, i.e. to the stabilizers of a single subspace of dimension $i$: taking $a_1=i$, $a_2=n-i$ gives the block upper triangular group with two diagonal blocks, which is the stabilizer of $k^i\subseteq k^n$, and the general $P_I$ is the intersection of these stabilizers over the cuts $i\in\Delta\smallsetminus I$, not over $I$. For $n\ge3$, the minimal proper parabolics strictly above $B$ are $P_{\{i\}}$, since singletons are the minimal nonempty proper subsets of the base. For $n\le2$ there is no proper parabolic strictly between $B$ and $G$; in particular, for $n=2$ the singleton gives $G$, rather than a proper parabolic. Finally, the simple-root reflections act on the characters $\chi_i$ by adjacent transpositions. Since they generate the Weyl group, its faithful lattice action is precisely $S_n$. The Bruhat cells of $G/B$ are indexed by $S_n$, and the length $n(w)$ equals the dimension of the cell by the length formula of [F3]. For the roots $\chi_i-\chi_j$ with $i<j$, the count $|\Phi^+\cap w\Phi^-|$ is the inversion number of $w^{-1}$. This equals the inversion number of $w$: $(i,j)\mapsto(w(j),w(i))$ bijects their inversion sets. Thus the count is $\#\{(i,j):i<j,\ w(i)>w(j)\}$ over every field. [F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

source_lines.47: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field and let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space of dimension $n\ge1$. The set $\mathrm{Fl}(V)$ of complete flags
source_lines.49: carries the structure of a smooth projective classical $k$-variety: it is the closed subvariety of the product of Grassmannians $\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}\mathbf{Gr}_i(V)$ cut out by the incidence conditions $V_i\subseteq V_{i+1}$, embedded in a product of projective spaces by Plücker coordinates. The group $\mathrm{GL}(V)$ acts transitively on $\mathrm{Fl}(V)$, the stabilizer of a flag is a closed subgroup scheme of $\mathrm{GL}(V)$, and the stabilizer of a complete flag is solvable.
source_lines.58: [F3] Incidence is closed: for $1\le i\le n-1$ the set $\{(W,W')\in\operatorname{Gr}(i,V)\times\operatorname{Gr}(i+1,V):W\subseteq W'\}$ is a closed subvariety of the product. In a standard affine chart of $\operatorname{Gr}(i+1,V)$ in which $W'$ is spanned by the rows of a matrix whose first $i+1$ columns form the identity, a complement of the chart locus is given by the vanishing of the Plücker coordinate, and $W\subseteq W'$ is expressed by the linear equations saying that a spanning matrix of $W$ has zero entries in the coordinates complementary to $W'$; these equations are polynomial in the chart coordinates of $W$ and glue over the charts of $\operatorname{Gr}(i,V)$. (Milne, Proposition 7.30, printed p. 146. No local item isolates this incidence statement.)
source_lines.72: 1.1 For $n=1$, the empty product is the one-point variety, there is a unique flag, and all incidence conditions are vacuous. For $n>1$, by [F1] each $\operatorname{Gr}(i,V)$ is a projective variety, and by [F2] the product $P=\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}\operatorname{Gr}(i,V)$ is a projective variety. By [F3] each incidence condition $V_i\subseteq V_{i+1}$ defines a closed subvariety, so their intersection $\mathrm{Fl}(V)\subseteq P$ is a closed subvariety; by [F4] it is projective, hence complete, and its Plücker embedding in the product of projective spaces is the restriction of the Plücker embeddings of the factors. [F1, F2, F3, F4]

source_lines.108: 4.1 Base change and finite flat normalization. Consider a cartesian square with $f:X\to Y$ proper and $g:Y'\to Y$ flat of pure relative dimension $n$, and write $f':X'=X\times_Y Y'\to Y'$ and $g':X'\to X$. For an integral $d$-dimensional $V\subseteq X$, put $W=\overline{f(V)}$ and $e=\dim V-\dim W$. If $e>0$, both $g^*f_*[V]$ and $f'_*g'^*[V]$ are zero: every component of the flat pullback of $V$ has dimension $d+n$, while its image has dimension at most $\dim W+n<d+n$. If $e=0$, set $m=[k(V):k(W)]$. For each component $W_i$ of $g^{-1}(W)$, let $C_i$ be the Artinian local ring of $W\times_Y Y'$ at its generic point. Flat pullback gives coefficient $\ell(C_i)$ on $[W_i]$. The generic algebra of $V\times_Y Y'$ over $C_i$ is $C_i\otimes_{k(W)}k(V)$, a free $C_i$-module of rank $m$. Decomposing it into its Artinian local factors shows that the sum of the generic lengths of the components above $W_i$, weighted by their function-field degrees over $k(W_i)$, is $m\ell(C_i)$. These are precisely the coefficients of $[W_i]$ in $f'_*g'^*[V]$ and $g^*f_*[V]$, respectively. Hence the base-change identity holds on cycles and therefore on Chow groups. Finally, if $f$ is finite flat of constant degree $n$ between integral schemes of the same dimension, then $f$ is dominant and $[k(X):k(Y)]=n$, so $f_*[X]=n[Y]$ by step 1.1. [F1, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

source_lines.49: 1.1 On a finite affine cover with affine intersections, quasi-coherent sections on each intersection are module localizations. A short exact sequence therefore gives a termwise exact sequence of Čech complexes, hence a long exact sequence of their cohomology by the elementary kernel/image diagram chase. The localization Čech complex for a principal cover of an affine scheme is exact in positive degrees: localizing it at any prime, one covering function is a unit and insertion of its index is a contracting homotopy. Its cohomology modules thus vanish at every prime, and vanish globally. Refining finite affine covers by principal covers and using this contraction in the rows or columns of the double Čech complex preserves their cohomology. In particular the standard cover may be used consistently for sheaves, exact sequences and closed-immersion pushforwards. Its complex has length $N$, so its cohomology vanishes above $N$. [F1, algebra]
source_lines.53: 2.1 For $N>0$, the Čech complex of $\mathcal O(d)$ on $\mathbb P_A^N$ decomposes into complexes indexed by Laurent monomials $T_0^{e_0}\cdots T_N^{e_N}$ with $\sum e_i=d$. Such a monomial appears on precisely the intersections whose index set contains $J=\{i:e_i<0\}$. If $J$ is empty, the simplex complex has one copy of $A$ in degree-zero cohomology. If $J$ is the full index set, it has one copy of $A$ in degree $N$. In every other case choose an index outside $J$; insertion of that index with the usual alternating sign is a contracting homotopy, so the complex is acyclic. Thus $H^0(\mathcal O(d))$ has the finite basis of monomials with all $e_i\ge0$, $H^N(\mathcal O(d))$ has the finite basis with all $e_i<0$, and all intermediate groups vanish. The top group is zero for $d\ge-N$. For $N=0$ the space is affine, its sole group is $A$ in degree zero for every twist, and the assertions follow directly. [step 1.1, algebra]

source_lines.90: 1.1 (Actual cosimplicial Hodge complexes.) Choose the smooth projective proper hypercover $a:Y_\bullet\to Y$ of [F1]. For sheaves of rational or complex vector spaces, construct the Godement resolution of [F10]. Its first functor $C^0$ is exact because stalks are exact and products of surjective linear maps are surjective under AC. In a short exact sequence of sheaves, the corresponding germ embeddings into $C^0$ form a diagram with exact rows and columns; the kernel-cokernel exact sequence makes the three cokernels short exact. Iteration proves that every successive cokernel functor, every $C^t$ and every $\Gamma C^t$ is exact, the last again being a product of stalks. In particular resolutions and global sections preserve filtration levels, their finite intersections and associated gradings. Their first-quadrant totals compute derived global sections: termwise flasque acyclicity from [F10] applies to each sheaf of the bounded de Rham complex, and each total diagonal is finite. Apply this construction on every $Y_p$ and put $K_{\mathbb Q}^{p,q}=\Gamma(Y_p,C^q(\mathbb Q_{Y_p}))$ and $K_{\mathbb C}^{p,q}=\bigoplus_{k+t=q}\Gamma(Y_p,C^t(\Omega^k_{Y_p}))$, for $p,q\ge0$, with $F^b$ given by $k\ge b$. These are the resolved global de Rham complexes, not the complex of global holomorphic forms. Godement pullback along each face is induced by pulling a germ collection at a point to the stalk over its image; the successive cokernels preserve these maps, so their composites obey the simplicial identities and preserve $F$. The constant inclusion $\mathbb Q\otimes\mathbb C\to\Omega^0$ gives the functorial rational comparison; on cohomology it is the scalar-extension comparison of [F4]. Exactness and acyclicity of the resolution show $H^q(K_{\mathbb C}^p)=H^q(Y_p;\mathbb C)$, with the holomorphic-degree image filtration, and $H^q(K_{\mathbb Q}^p)=H^q(Y_p;\mathbb Q)$. The compact Hodge theorem [F4] gives pure weight $q$ and Hodge-de Rham $E_1$ degeneration on each smooth projective component. The latter makes the actual internal differential $F$-strict: if $dx\in F^b$, degeneration lifts the leading lower-filtration class of $x$ to a cycle up to a higher-filtration term and a boundary; subtracting the cycle and boundary raises the preimage filtration without changing $dx$, and finite induction supplies a preimage in $F^b$. This proves differential strictness directly. Thus every level is an actual weight-zero rational Hodge complex. Each internal total diagonal is finite, and $F^{q+1}K^{p,q}=0$, so [F3] applies to its first-quadrant simple complex, giving the mixed Hodge structure and $E_1^{p,q}=H^q(Y_p;\mathbb Q)$, $E_2$ degeneration and $\operatorname{Gr}^W_qH^n(sK)=E_2^{n-q,q}$. The terms have $p=n-q\ge0$, so weights are at most $n$, and the finitely many $E_1^{p,q}$ entries on every total diagonal are finite-dimensional by [F4]. Descent [F2] identifies the rational simple cohomology naturally with $H^n(Y;\mathbb Q)$, carrying this structure. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F9, F10, construct, algebra]
